cases.reason: The canonical line the reference encoder emits — the byte-exact form every binding must reproduce.
Every optional member populated at once, in the fixed member order §4 requires.

§4 rule 5 requires error's members be emitted code-then-retriable, but every other case already supplies them in that order, so a binding emitting them in input-insertion order passed the whole corpus. This case supplies retriable first.
fields keys are sorted ascending by code point regardless of the caller's insertion order.

The case file's fields.ms is the literal 118.0, an integral-valued JSON number — a JSON number whose value is integral must be accepted and encoded without a fractional part, whatever host type carried it. Python's json.loads parses 118.0 as a float; a binding that rejects a non-int host type rather than testing the value fails this case even though JavaScript's own JSON.parse silently collapses the same literal to 118 and cannot see the distinction at all.

The case file's fields.rate is the literal 1.5, genuinely fractional — the complement of the integral-value rule: a value whose magnitude is not a whole number is refused as invalid-field-value, not silently truncated or coerced.

The case file's fields.n is the literal 1e400 — JSON has no NaN/Infinity literal, so a value overflowing to Infinity (JavaScript) or inf (Python) is the expressible form of the case. Non-finite numbers MUST be rejected as invalid-field-value; a generator that serializes this input through JSON.stringify before writing the fixture collapses it to null, which is indistinguishable from fields-null-rejected.json and leaves this rule with zero coverage — which is exactly what happened here in an earlier draft and is why this file's input must be edited by hand, never regenerated.

The case file's fields.n is the literal 9007199254740993 (2^53+1) — a fields value MUST NOT exceed +-(2^53-1), the one bound both JavaScript and Python can hold exactly. JavaScript's own JSON.parse cannot represent 9007199254740993 exactly and silently rounds it to an adjacent double when this file is loaded, but the verdict (invalid-field-value) holds under either neighbor since both are still outside the safe-integer range; a Python binding parses the exact value 9007199254740993 and must reach the identical verdict.
2^53-1 is exactly the bound, and the bound is inclusive.
The +-(2^53-1) bound is symmetric; a negative integer is an ordinary accepted value.
Zero is an ordinary integer, not a sentinel for absence.

The case file's fields.n is the literal -0.0. Regression pin on the integral-float narrowing: naive Python emits -0.0 where JavaScript's own JSON.stringify emits 0, and a binding that skips normalizing through the integral check would pass every other numeric case and fail only here — but only if the fixture's input is genuinely -0.0 on disk. A generator that serializes this input through JSON.stringify before writing the fixture collapses it to plain 0, making the fixture byte-identical to fields-zero-accepted.json and pinning nothing; this file's input is therefore edited by hand, never regenerated.
A boolean is one of the two accepted fields value types.
null is neither a boolean nor an integer, so it is refused rather than treated as absence.
fields is a flat map; a nested object value is refused.
An array is neither a boolean nor an integer.
An empty fields object is well-formed — zero entries is not the same failure as fields being absent or non-object.
fields must itself be a JSON object before its keys or values are inspected at all.
A fields key must match ^[a-z][a-z0-9]*$; an uppercase letter is refused.
Underscore is not in the fields key alphabet.
Sixteen is the published maximum, and the bound is inclusive.
Seventeen well-formed keys exceeds the maximum and is refused as too-many-fields, once every key and value has already passed.

Seventeen field keys where one is invalid MUST report invalid-field-key, not too-many-fields — §5 orders the key-pattern row before the count row, and this is the only case that can tell the two orders apart, since fields-seventeen-rejected uses seventeen VALID keys.

Seventeen field values where one is invalid MUST report invalid-field-value, not too-many-fields — §5 orders the value-pattern row before the count row too, one row below the key-pattern row fields-bad-key-with-seventeen-keys.json pins. A binding that checks the count before checking values passes fields-seventeen-rejected (all-valid values) and fails only here.

invalid-field-key and invalid-field-value are two SEPARATE passes over the whole object: every key is checked before any value is, so a combined-fault input must still report invalid-field-key even when a bad value would be reached first under insertion order. A single interleaved key-then-value pass reports invalid-field-value here and fails only this case.
A field key containing / must render as ~1 in the JSON Pointer path per RFC 6901 — an unescaped binding emits /fields/a/b, which reads as a nested member that was never sent.

An unknown member is rejected, not ignored — the redaction guarantee. Reason text must cite negotiation/cases/hello-unknown-member.json, which requires the opposite: the hello frame is open, the diagnostic envelope is closed, and the two documents pin opposite behaviors on purpose.
null is valid JSON but not an object, and must be refused before any member is inspected.
An array is valid JSON, array-shaped, but not an object.
ts is MUST; its absence is invalid-ts, not a separate missing-member reason.
The ts pattern requires exactly three fractional digits; Python's isoformat() default produces six and must be refused, not silently truncated.
The ts pattern requires a literal Z, not a +00:00 offset — even the obvious timespec="milliseconds" fix still fails, since the offset form itself is wrong.
The pattern is case-sensitive; a lowercase t or z is refused.
The fractional-seconds group is not optional in the ts pattern.
The ts pattern is spelled [0-9], never \d, so a Unicode digit that looks like an ASCII one is refused rather than silently accepted by a Unicode-aware regex engine.
debug is one of the four accepted level tokens.
info is one of the four accepted level tokens.
warn is one of the four accepted level tokens.
error is one of the four accepted level tokens.
A level outside the published four-value set is refused as invalid-level.
Level tokens are case-sensitive lowercase.
extensionId must be non-empty; the empty string is refused.
The rule is emptiness, not blankness — no trim is defined, so a single space is a non-empty, accepted value.
Non-ASCII characters are NOT escaped in the output — pins ensure_ascii=False for a conformant Python encoder.
The event pattern is lowercase-only.
Underscore is not in the event pattern's alphabet.
Hyphen is not in the event pattern's alphabet.
Consecutive dots produce an empty segment, which the pattern disallows.
Each segment must start with a letter, not a digit.
audit is one of the two accepted kind values.
A kind outside {diagnostic, audit} is refused as invalid-kind.
correlationId is optional; its absence means "not attributable to one request" and the output line simply omits the member.
null and absence are different: a binding whose accessor collapses them (e.g. dict.get()) would wrongly accept this.
64 characters is the published maximum, and the bound is inclusive.
65 characters exceeds the maximum and is refused.
@ is not in the correlationId alphabet — the bound is a speed bump against free text, not a length check alone.
code is the only required error member.
code is required whenever error is present.
error carries no message member — a stack trace's cousin is still free text.
error carries no stack member — a stack trace is free text with extra steps, carrying file paths and interpolated values.
Two faults at once (a malformed ts and an unknown member) must report unknown-member — closedness is checked before any per-member value check, pinning §5's reason order end to end.

The encoded line MUST NOT exceed IPC_MAX_LINE_BYTES; this is line-too-long's only producer in the corpus, since §5.1 makes the reason encode-only and no parse case may expect it. Generated (repeat), one octet over the limit, and paired with line-at-limit-accepted.json to pin the boundary from both sides.

A line of exactly IPC_MAX_LINE_BYTES octets is accepted — the limit is inclusive, and the implementation's check is strictly greater-than. A binding using >= instead would reject this line while passing every other case, since line-too-long-rejected.json alone only pins the over-limit side.
The canonical line round-trips: parsing it recovers the event, without the nimbus discriminator.
not-json is the only reason checked before the table's own rows — there is no parsed value to classify until the line has parsed as JSON at all.

not-object (the table's row 1) is reached in its normal position and checked before wrong-message (inserted immediately after it) — an array has no nimbus member to be right or wrong about, so a binding that checked wrong-message first would need one to exist before it could even ask. No other parse case in this corpus is syntactically valid JSON and still not an object, so this is the only executable form of that ordering.

wrong-message is inserted immediately after not-object and before every remaining row of the table, unknown-member included — a well-formed envelope for a different message is refused before its members are checked.
wrong-message covers both a present-but-wrong nimbus and an absent one — an empty object has no discriminator to match.
Once a line is known to be diag-discriminated JSON, the remaining table rows apply exactly as on encode — an unknown member is refused on parse too, not only on encode.
warn's index is greater than info's, so warn meets an info threshold.
A level meets its own threshold — the comparison is >=, not >.
debug's index is less than info's, so debug does not meet an info threshold.

An unpublished level answers meets: false rather than throwing — Python's tuple.index() raises where JavaScript's indexOf returns -1, and a binding that ports index() directly raises here while passing every case built only from the four published levels.
The mirror of level-invalid-level-position-below-threshold.json on the threshold argument — both positions must be checked independently, so a binding that only guards level still fails here.
